title_guess: Basel accords part 2: risk-weighted assets, capital adequacy ratio (CAR/CRAR), tier 1 and tier 2 capital, Basel II's three pillars, Basel III's buffers (LCR, NSFR, CCCB, CCB) and India's latest ratios
recurring_cast: left sidebar kept from part 1 (E26): bank_building over the three risk names (credit, market, operational), each lit or struck as the accords cover it
brand_logo (RBI coin emblem; BIS logo in the recall panel)
coin_jar ('How much?' jar of coins with a rupee coin on top: the capital cushion, later the CAR container)
pillar (the bank standing on one pillar, then three, then with an iron middle pillar)
five Basel III containers in a row: coin_jar (CAR), glass jar of coins (LCR), money_bag sack (NSFR), piggy_bank (CCCB), briefcase (CCB)
pale panel in the middle where each container is zoomed and explained
running_examples: a bank's loans: unsecured 1000 Rs at 50% risk = 500, secured 4000 Rs at 10% risk = 400, RWA = 900 Rs (capital at 8% of it, 72 Rs, is never worked out)
CAR 8% recommended by BCBS in 1988; India adopted Basel I in 1999 with CRAR 9% (9% shown, spoken only as '1% more')
car analogy: front guard takes small knocks (tier 1), airbags save you in a big crash but the car is towed (tier 2)
Basel II: tier 1 at least 4% of RWA; Basel III: CAR 9.5%, tier 1 from 4.5% to 6%, LCR 100% over 30 days, NSFR for 1 year, CCB 2.5% of RWA
Financial Stability Report December 2022: CRAR of all scheduled commercial banks 16.0% (Sep 2022), and 6.9 read out from a tier 1 leverage ratio chart

best_moments.why: the bank standing on a single 'minimum capital' pillar gets two more pillars on the word 'pillars', and the market and operational risk rows light up in the sidebar: what Basel II added and why, in one picture
for Basel III the middle pillar turns black (iron) on the spoken word: 'strengthen pillar 1' shown as a material change

five everyday containers (jar, glass jar, sack, piggy bank, briefcase) line up under the bank, each later lifted into the middle panel and explained, and at 781 s all five send arrows up to the bank: a set of abstract buffers made concrete and kept on screen as a visual index
car analogy: a front guard labelled tier I meets an obstacle, airbags labelled tier II open in a bigger crash, then the car leaves the canvas: tier 1 vs tier 2 by consequence

bank lends to a crowd of customers, a red circle with a DEFAULT stamp covers part of the crowd, and a dotted 'unexpected losses' line runs back to the bank, which then drops coins into a jar: credit risk to capital cushion in one chain
the worked example is built row by row next to the risk table: loan amounts, risk %, risk amounts, and a 900 Rs bubble with a line to RWA

weak_moments.why: tier 1 and tier 2 components are a bullet list, and several items need checking: SLR assets and total liquid cash listed under disclosed reserves, retained earnings and fixed assets listed under tier 2

Basel III numbers need checking: CAR '9.5%' and a newly added 'Tier III capital' (Basel III is usually described as removing tier 3); tier 1 '4.5% to 6%' is spoken but not shown, and contradicts the '4%' shown for Basel II

an imported chart titled 'Tier I Leverage Ratio' (6.9 for all SCBs) is read out as the tier 1 capital percentage set by RBI; the CRAR chart's 16% is likewise called a value RBI has applied, though it is the banks' achieved ratio
the note 'every SCB has to maintain CAR or CRAR of 9%' is on screen, but the voice never says 9; the India adoption year 1999 also needs checking (capital adequacy norms began in the early 1990s)
about 11 s of speech is missing from the transcript (one word stretched over 77-89 s) while the canvas rebuilds into the risk table
the voice says to break the piggy bank in bad times, but the picture only shows two text arrows (add capital / take out capital); the piggy bank is never broken
risk categories are a five-row table with category numbers only; the example's mapping (unsecured loans 50%, secured loans 10%) needs checking against Basel I weights

segments.teaches: recall of part 1: banks face credit, market and operational risk; RBI passes on the Basel accords made by the Basel Committee (BCBS) of the Bank for International Settlements in Switzerland; Basel I 1988, II 2004, III 2010

elements.what: bank with the three red risk names under it (left panel)
RBI coin emblem in a yellow middle band, dotted arrow to the bank
BIS logo with a 'Switzerland' banner and the bank's name; BCBS strip under it
'Basel accords' list: Basel I 1988, II 2004, III 2010, dotted line back to RBI
grey boxes thrown round the bank panel (9.8 s) and the BIS/BCBS panel (15 s) as each is recalled

segments.notes: Reuses the part-1 overview board (E26). Each part of the board is boxed in grey as the voice recalls it. The voice says 'Bank of International Settlements' (the name is Bank for International Settlements).
segments.idea: the Basel rules come from an international committee and reach Indian banks through RBI, to deal with three kinds of bank risk
segments.shown_as: the finished overview board from part 1 (bank with three risks, RBI coin, BIS logo with the Basel list) stays on screen while grey boxes highlight the bank's risks and then the BIS/BCBS block as each is recalled

segments.teaches: Basel I deals with credit risk: some borrowers do not repay and nobody knows how many, so losses are unexpected; each bank must set money aside to absorb them; the question is how much

elements.what: 'BASEL I' heading chip
'Credit risk' row lit in the left sidebar
bank with a 'Loan' arrow to a crowd of customers
dark crowd of customer heads
red circle over part of the crowd with a 'DEFAULT' stamp and 'How many?'
dotted red 'UNEXPECTED LOSSES' line from the defaulters back to the bank
down-arrow from the bank to a jar of coins
banks should save enough capital to meet obligations and absorb unexpected losses; 'How much?' under the jar

segments.notes: 5 change events. The default circle and stamp land about 1 s before 'customers ... cannot repay' is said; the jar with the 'How much?' question becomes the thread that the next three segments answer.
segments.idea: because some borrowers will default in numbers nobody can predict, a bank must keep a cushion of capital; the open question is its size
segments.shown_as: the bank sends a loan arrow to a crowd; a red circle stamped DEFAULT covers part of the crowd and a dotted 'unexpected losses' line runs back to the bank; the bank then drops coins down into a jar labelled 'How much?'
segments.example: a crowd of borrowers, some of whom default

segments.teaches: Basel I sorts a bank's assets into five risk categories (0%, 10%, 20%, 50%, 100%); the bank classifies its loans by this table and computes its risk-weighted assets (RWA)

elements.what: bank moves to the top; the 'How much?' jar shrinks to the bottom-right corner
blue down-arrow from the bank to the table
'Asset categorisation': type of loan (category 1-5) against risk (0, 10, 20, 50, 100%)
blue arrow from the table to 'RWA - Risk Weighted Asset'

segments.notes: Hidden transcript gap: one word is stretched over 77.3-88.6 s, so the words spoken while the table frame appears are lost. Category rows are numbered only; what kind of asset sits in each category is never shown.
segments.idea: not all loans are equally risky, so each counts only by its risk weight
segments.shown_as: the default picture clears; the bank rises to the top with a blue arrow down into a two-column table whose rows fill in as five categories with 0-100% risk; a blue arrow then points from the table to 'RWA'

segments.teaches: worked example: unsecured loans 1000 Rs fall in category 4 (50%) and secured loans 4000 Rs in category 2 (10%); risk amounts 500 + 400 = 900 Rs, which is the bank's RWA; a percentage of RWA kept safe is the capital adequacy ratio (CAR)

elements.what: two arrows from the bank: 'Unsecured loans' to '1000 Rs', 'Secured loans' to '4000 Rs'
'Risk %' column (50%, 10%) and 'Risk associated' column (500 Rs, 400 Rs) added beside the amounts
orange '900 Rs' bubble with a line down to RWA
'How much?' under the jar outlined
RWA, a down-arrow through a '%' box into the jar, labelled CAR

segments.notes: About 9 change events, each number landing within about 1 s of its word. The example stops at RWA = 900 Rs: the capital it needs (8% of 900 = 72 Rs) is never worked out. The secured/unsecured weights need checking against Basel I.
segments.idea: a bank's risk-weighted assets are its loans weighted by riskiness; the capital cushion is a percentage of that figure
segments.shown_as: two loan arrows from the bank carry 1000 and 4000; a risk % column (50, 10) and a risk-amount column (500, 400) write on beside them; an orange 900 bubble drops a line to RWA; 'How much?' is outlined, and a % box appears between RWA and the jar, named CAR

segments.teaches: CAR = the share of RWA a bank must hold as capital; BCBS recommended 8% in 1988; India adopted Basel I in 1999 and calls it CRAR; India keeps it 1% above Basel (9%) for extra stability

elements.what: bank, down-arrow, RWA, '%' box, jar 'How much?'; 'CAR' tag on the % box
'8% CAR - recommended by BCBS in year 1988'
India map with 'India adopted Basel I norms in 1999', dotted arrow from the 8% note
RBI coin with 'every SCB has to maintain CAR or CRAR of 9%', dotted arrow from the map

segments.notes: 4 change events. The 9% is shown but never spoken (the voice says '1% more than Basel'); CRAR is spoken but appears only in this note. The adoption year 1999 needs checking.
segments.idea: capital needed = a fixed percentage of risk-weighted assets; India's rule is stricter than the Basel minimum
segments.shown_as: the table clears to a vertical chain: bank, RWA, a % box tagged CAR, the jar; an '8% (BCBS 1988)' note sits on the % box, a dotted arrow hops to an India map ('adopted 1999') and on to the RBI coin with 'CAR or CRAR of 9%'

segments.teaches: the minimum capital requirement has two parts: tier 1 absorbs losses while the bank keeps working; tier 2 can absorb losses only if the bank winds up, since it is not liquid

elements.what: bank, blue arrow to the coin jar now labelled 'Minimum Capital Requirement'
two arrows from the jar to 'Tier II Capital' (left) and 'Tier I Capital' (right)
under tier I: absorbs losses without the bank stopping; under tier II: absorbs losses in a winding-up

segments.notes: 3 change events, each label on its word.
segments.idea: capital comes in a first line that can be used at once and a second line that is only usable when the bank closes
segments.shown_as: the jar, now named minimum capital requirement, splits by two arrows into tier II and tier I chips, and a one-line definition writes on under each as it is spoken

segments.teaches: analogy: a car's front guard takes small knocks and breaks so the car is safe (tier 1); in a bigger crash the airbags open and save you (tier 2), but the car must be towed away

elements.what: white car with two passengers at the bottom of the canvas
'Tier I' label on the front guard
black obstacle at the front guard, changing for the bigger crash
airbags opening in front of the passengers, 'Tier II' label

segments.notes: About 6 change events. The car simply disappears at 308.4 s while the voice says it must be towed behind a truck; no tow is drawn.
segments.idea: tier 1 lets the bank carry on after a small loss; tier 2 saves depositors in a big loss but the bank stops
segments.shown_as: a car with a 'Tier I' front guard meets an obstacle; in the bigger crash airbags labelled 'Tier II' burst open in front of the passengers; then the car leaves the canvas as the voice says it has to be towed

segments.teaches: tier 1 has more loss-absorbing capacity and is more reliable and liquid, so RBI treats it as the core measure (core capital) of a bank's strength; tier 1 = shareholders' equity and disclosed reserves; tier 2 = undisclosed reserves, retained earnings, fixed assets; using tier 2 means the bank almost has to close

elements.what: 'Debt absorption capacity of tier I is more than tier II' (then removed)
RBI coin with dotted arrows from both tiers and 'RBI assesses financial strength from tier I and II'
tier I note: financial capital, more reliable and liquid; 'Core measure / Core capital' tag
green-square bullets under tier I: stockholders' equity, disclosed reserves (sub-bullets SLR assets, total liquid cash)
bullets under tier II: undisclosed reserves, retained earnings, fixed assets

segments.notes: About 12 change events, mostly bullets on their words; 'retained earnings' appears inside an 11 s transcript gap (392.8-404.1 s). Component lists need checking: SLR assets and cash are not normally counted as disclosed reserves, and retained earnings are usually tier 1; fixed assets are not capital (only their revaluation reserves can count in tier 2).
segments.idea: which kinds of bank money count as first-line (core) capital and which as second-line
segments.shown_as: a note on tier I's greater loss capacity writes on and clears; dotted arrows run from both tier chips down to the RBI coin (RBI judges strength from them); a 'core capital' tag sits on tier I and green bullet lists grow under each tier as components are named

segments.teaches: recap of Basel I: one focus only, the minimum capital requirement of 8% of RWA in two tiers; it covers credit risk but not market and operational risk, so banks following it still failed

elements.what: bank standing on one tall pillar labelled 'Minimum Capital Requirement'
'8% of RWA' and 'Tier II / Tier I Capital' chips under the pillar
'Market risk' and 'Operational risk' struck through in the sidebar

segments.notes: The tier diagram fades and the pillar picture rises before the pillar metaphor is spoken (it is first said at 480 s). Transcript gap 462.7-466.5 s as the risks are struck.
segments.idea: Basel I stood on one support and left two of the three risks uncovered
segments.shown_as: the old diagram fades; the bank now stands on a single pillar named minimum capital requirement with '8% of RWA' and the two tier chips at its foot, and the market and operational risk rows in the sidebar are struck through

segments.teaches: Basel II (2004): a bank cannot stand on one pillar, so two more were added: supervisory review (the bank's internal processes and systems) and market discipline (stricter disclosure for transparency), to cover market and operational risk; pillar 1 now also requires tier 1 of at least 4% of RWA, the rest being tier 2; even so, banks fell in the 2008 crisis

elements.what: 'BASEL II [Published in 2004]' heading
two more pillars added either side of the central one
'Supervisory Review' and 'Market Discipline' chips with arrows to the side pillars
strikes removed; market risk then operational risk rows lit in the sidebar
notes: supervisory review focuses on internal processes and systems; market discipline means disclosure for transparency
'4% of RWA' under tier I and 'Remaining %' under tier II

segments.notes: About 10 change events, each within about 1 s of its word. The 2008 failure is only spoken; the picture does not show the pillars failing.
segments.idea: Basel II kept the capital rule and added supervision and disclosure so that all three risks are covered
segments.shown_as: two side pillars appear under the bank on the word 'pillars', each tagged (supervisory review, market discipline); as the voice says what they cover, the market and operational risk rows in the sidebar light up; short notes explain each pillar, and '4% of RWA' is written under tier I

segments.teaches: Basel III (2010): the middle pillar must be made of iron, i.e. banks cannot rely on minimum capital alone and must keep money in several other places for bad times; five containers stand for five Basel III terms (CAR, LCR, NSFR, CCCB, CCB)

elements.what: 'BASEL III' heading
middle pillar turns black (iron)
row of five containers under the pillars: coin jar, glass jar of coins, rupee sack, piggy bank, briefcase
labels CAR, LCR, NSFR, CCCB, CCB under the containers

segments.notes: 4 change events; the voice names the containers in Hindi (dabba, bori, gullak, briefcase) while they are on screen, then the labels appear on 'different terms'.
segments.idea: after 2008 the capital rule was hardened and banks were told to keep several separate reserves for bad times
segments.shown_as: the middle pillar turns black (iron) on its word; then five everyday containers pop up in a row at the foot of the pillars and get their acronyms written under them
segments.example: five containers for CAR, LCR, NSFR, CCCB, CCB

segments.teaches: Basel III raises the minimum capital requirement (CAR) to 9.5%, adds a tier 3 to supplement tiers 1 and 2, and raises the tier 1 minimum from 4.5% to 6% (as narrated; needs checking)

elements.what: the coin jar lifts out of the row into a pale panel
'9.5%' and 'CAR' beside the jar
'Tier I Capital', 'Tier II Capital', then 'Tier III Capital'

segments.notes: 4 change events. Tier 1 '4.5% to 6%' is spoken but not shown. Facts to check: Basel III's total minimum is usually given as 8% (10.5% with the conservation buffer; RBI 9% and 11.5%), and Basel III is usually described as abolishing tier 3.
segments.idea: Basel III asks for more capital than before
segments.shown_as: the CAR jar slides up from the row into a pale panel with '9.5% CAR' beside it and tier chips (I, II, then III) written under it

segments.teaches: LCR (liquidity coverage ratio): a bank must hold enough high-quality liquid assets to survive 30 days of severe stress; it is a ratio, HQLA divided by total net cash flows over 30 days, x100, and Basel III asks for 100%

elements.what: glass jar of coins lifted into the panel, labelled 'Liquidity Coverage Ratio - LCR'
HQLAs to survive an acute stress scenario lasting 30 days
'30 DAYS'
LCR = HQLAs / total net cash flows (of 30 days) x 100

segments.notes: 5 change events. The voice says to fill the jar and close its lid, but no lid is drawn. The 100% target is spoken but not written. The standard denominator is net cash outflows.
segments.idea: a bank must keep enough easily sold assets to cover a month of heavy withdrawals, measured as a ratio
segments.shown_as: the glass coin jar rises from the row into the panel with its name; a callout and a '30 DAYS' tag write on, then the ratio formula appears under it with 'of 30 days' added beneath the denominator
segments.example: HQLA equal to 30 days' net cash flows gives LCR 100%

segments.teaches: NSFR (net stable funding ratio): enough stable funding to get through a whole year of bad times; a short stress is handled by LCR, a longer one by NSFR; one year counts as medium term

elements.what: rupee sack lifted into the panel, labelled 'Net Stable Funding Ratio - NSFR'
'1 Year'
reliable source of finance to fund bank activities for medium-term resilience

segments.notes: 4 change events; the callout comes about 3 s before 'medium term' is said. No formula is given for NSFR (unlike LCR).
segments.idea: beyond the first month, a bank needs funding that will stay for a year
segments.shown_as: the LCR jar drops back and the rupee sack rises into the panel with its name; '1 Year' writes on beneath and a callout on medium-term funding draws in

segments.teaches: CCCB (countercyclical capital buffer): put capital into the piggy bank when credit is growing fast (good times) and break it to take capital out in stress; when to start and when to release is decided by the central bank (RBI in India), not the bank

elements.what: piggy bank lifted into the panel, labelled 'Countercyclical Capital Buffer - CCCB'
'ADD CAPITAL - period of excessive credit growth' with a dotted arrow into the piggy bank
dotted arrow out to 'TAKE OUT CAPITAL - during the period of stress'
CCCB set by national regulatory authorities

segments.notes: 5 change events, each on its words. The piggy bank is never broken or filled in the picture; only labelled arrows show in and out.
segments.idea: save extra capital in boom years and release it in bad years, on the regulator's signal
segments.shown_as: the piggy bank rises into the panel; an 'add capital' label on the left sends a dotted arrow into it and a dotted arrow leaves it to 'take out capital' on the right; a callout says the regulator sets it
segments.example: good times: fill; bad times: break

segments.teaches: CCB (capital conservation buffer): 2.5% of risk-weighted assets kept in the briefcase; all this money is there to serve the bank in its bad times

elements.what: briefcase lifted into the panel, labelled 'Capital Conservation Buffer'
'2.5% of RWA'
panel clears; the five containers in a row each send an arrow up to the bank

segments.notes: 4 change events. The closing arrows from all five containers to the bank work as a silent recap of Basel III.
segments.idea: a fixed extra slice of capital is kept for bad times, and every buffer exists to protect the bank
segments.shown_as: the briefcase rises into the panel with '2.5% of RWA'; then the panel empties and five arrows run from the jar, glass jar, sack, piggy bank and briefcase up to the bank

segments.teaches: where India stands (Financial Stability Report, December 2022): CRAR of all scheduled commercial banks 16% (also shown for public, private and foreign banks); 6.9% read out as the tier 1 figure; both above Basel recommendations

elements.what: imported grouped bar chart 'Capital to Risk-weighted Assets Ratio': PSBs, PVBs, FBs, all SCBs for Mar-21, Sep-21, Mar-22, Sep-22 (14.5, 17.2, 18.0, 16.0 labelled), source line FSR Dec 2022
second imported chart 'Tier I Leverage Ratio' (5.2, 9.0, 10.3, 6.9 labelled)

segments.notes: Sidebar risks unhighlighted. The second chart is a leverage ratio, but the voice reads 6.9 as the tier 1 capital percentage set by RBI; the 16% is the banks' achieved ratio, spoken as a value RBI has applied. Only the all-SCB values are spoken.
segments.idea: Indian banks currently hold more capital than the Basel minimum
segments.shown_as: the canvas cuts to a report bar chart of CRAR by bank group and date, then to a leverage-ratio bar chart; nothing is pointed at or highlighted
segments.example: CRAR 16.0% (all SCBs, Sep 2022); 6.9 from the leverage ratio chart
